cards.title: Abduction – Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: Gluteus Medius (Glutes/Hips) – Hip horizontal abduction

sections.heading: Synergists
items: Gluteus Minimus (Glutes/Hips) – Hip horizontal abduction
Gluteus Maximus – lateral fibers (Glutes/Hips) – Hip horizontal abduction
Piriformis – Hip horizontal abduction

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: Seat back is typically standardized at position 6 or 7 to maintain a more upright position
Thigh pad width determines starting point and lower turnaround, thus a gap is never needed
Pads should be as snug as possible without discomfort; slight compression of soft tissue may be desirable for increased ROM
If client has a history of hip issues or reports discomfort, slightly wider pad settings may be warranted
Subjects with larger hips/legs typically require wider pad settings; smaller individuals narrower settings
Movement arms must be pulled apart manually during client entry
If weight is too heavy to allow arms to be pulled apart manually, wait until client is seated to load weight stack
When setting weight post-entry, assist movement arms fully closed to allow selector pin placement; take additional care due to soft tissue compression

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Chest up, butt back, seat belt secured around waist (not over femurs or restricting hips), head neutral, feet and ankles relaxed
Hands on handles for balance—not for anchoring
Encourage anterior pelvic tilt facilitated by upright chest and slight lumbar arch

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: Load Up
From lower turnaround, cue client to lift chest, maintain neutral head, hands on handles, and gradually apply outward pressure through the knees
Instructor observes closely during initial load; brief affirmation such as “good” or “yes, just like that” as positive feedback
Concentric Phase / Upper Turnaround
Client drives knees apart “as far as comfortably possible” while lifting chest and arching back
Brief 1-2 second pause on first two reps and a 2–3 second squeeze from third rep onward
Instructor clicks at precise moment duration of squeeze is completed
Eccentric Phase
Click is immediately followed by instruction to “ease out, do not speed up”
Cue first lower turnaround before it is reached with language such as “touch and go,” “be continuous,” or “seamlessly change directions”
Always provide a cue on the first eccentric phase of the set to establish expectation for lower turn
Lower Turnaround
Movement should be continuous at the bottom with no pause—“touch and go”
Maintain chest up by leaning back and using handles for leverage (pushing down, not pulling up to anchor)
Execution
One continuous pace throughout
First two reps should have a brief 1-2 second pause in contracted position
Reps three and beyond include a 2–3 second squeeze at top
Verbal cues should guide HOW to squeeze, not just “squeeze”
Example verbiage
“Lift your chest, arch your back, continue to drive out through your knees as if the movement continues…keep breathing, keep still, [click], ease out”
“Keeping your head still, drive your knees apart as hard as you can…there, lock it in place…breathe freely…[click], ease out”
Only full reps (full contraction) are recorded on client charts
Partial reps may still be useful for stimulus if performed under control and subject is advanced/tolerant, especially near failure
For new clients, full ROM for a limited number of reps can be sufficient stimulus without going to failure
Encourage consistent pace with increasing effort to offset fatigue and to maintain tension

sections.heading: Notes
items: Watch for pinch points when loading/unloading clients; pull movement arms apart by ends of padding and return slowly as client lifts legs
Ensure client hands are clear of rocking/tilting thigh pads
Expect variability in client range of motion; encourage full ROM through safe abduction
Use first 2–3 reps to assess individual ROM and adjust coaching accordingly
Ensure limited ROM is not due to excessive weight or poor execution understanding
Instruct clients to drive through knees even if pads are not contacting them directly
Driving through knees is simpler to coach than through the femur, though the femur is the actual lever
Clients with hip replacements or other hip pathologies may not tolerate abduction
Conservative approach is to omit the exercise entirely or implement Timed Static Contraction (TSC) protocol
TSC Protocol
Pin weight too heavy to move with movement arm near midpoint
Instruct client to press outward statically
30 sec @ 50% effort
30 sec @ 75% effort
30 sec @ 100% effort
Performed at least weekly over months, this builds meaningful strength and potential for dynamic reintroduction
Expect carryover of ~15 degrees in either direction from static point
Progression Considerations
While learning Continuous Tension, lighter weight may result in higher reps and longer time under load
This may become counterproductive due to discomfort before stimulus is achieved
Over time, strive for perfect form with a slightly heavier load (goal: failure in ≤10 reps)
Target 6-second positive, 6-second negative reps
If subject demonstrates appropriate control and understanding, intensity can be increased sooner

cards.title: Abs – Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: Rectus Abdominis – Spinal Flexion/Posterior Pelvic Tilt

sections.heading: Synergists
items: External Obliques – Spinal Flexion
Transverse Abdominis – Hollowing (supports abdominal wall)
Pelvic Floor – Pelvis stabilization (in coordination with TA)
Rectus Femoris – Hip Flexion
Psoas – Hip Flexion

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: Set the weight stack prior to client entry; a standard gap of 6 is typical but may vary by machine and location as determined by Studio Leader and MSF Corporate
Ensure the movement arm (roller pad) is upright and locked; it only rests forward and will fall forward if not secured
Instructor must control the movement arm throughout the set, especially during client entry and exit
Determine seat pad height beginning with aligning the client’s iliac crest with the top of the roller pad at the back of the seat
Practical alignment must consider client height (torso length) and size of hip girdle; consider if they are too far above or below movement arm pad
Move femur restraint away from the seat to allow for client entry/exit
Instruct client to avoid contact with the movement arm when entering; keep arm in locked position and hold it securely in rear position during entry
Set foot placement on the fixed footplate to approximate knee angle with the femur restraint (knee pad) angle
With feet on the platform, adjust femur restraint so that pads straddle the knee caps evenly
Femur restraint should rest snugly above and below the knee, flush against femur and tibia, with slight wiggle room and no gaps
Unlock movement arm and carefully lower it into position in front of client once client is seated
Instruct client to lean back and lift arms over roller pad as it comes down; pad should rest in armpits or as close as comfortably possible
Client should bring elbows together and place hands in front of head in a “prayer” position
Start movement in the upper turnaround (contracted position) with instructor assisting client and movement arm into position
Instructor cues client to tighten abdominals and then gradually transfers control of the load while keeping the movement arm stationary

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Instructor assists client and movement arm into contracted position
Client increases abdominal effort while instructor gradually releases assistance, ensuring control throughout the transfer
Instructor gives a cue like “thaaat…iiisss…yyyours” to signify load transfer completion

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: Eccentric Phase
Instruct client to “slowly begin to lower the weight by uncurling the spine from the bottom up”
Cue client before reaching lower turnaround to “uncurl far enough to allow the weights to barely touch before changing directions and curling/tightening back down”
Always provide a cue on the first eccentric phase of the set to establish expectation at lower turn
Lower Turnaround
Before weights touch, cue client to “immediately” or “seamlessly” reverse direction once they do touch
“Immediate” indicates prompt transition, but not a sudden one
Concentric Phase
Instruct client to “begin to curl back down one vertebrae at a time from the top down toward their lap (or hip crease)” or “begin to draw their rib cage down to their pelvis”
Cue client to “tighten your abdominals and round your back…” to describe anatomical intent
Upper Turnaround
Concentric movement ends when abdomen is fully contracted—not necessarily when the movement arm reaches the top of the legs
Emphasize that goal is contraction of targeted musculature, not full range of motion of the machine
Brief pause at upper turnaround on first two reps, with a 2–3 second squeeze beginning with the third rep
Verbal cues for squeeze: “keep rounding, keep breathing, [click], ease out” or “tighten down hard, lock it in place, [click], ease out”
Always describe HOW to “squeeze” as it may not be instinctive for most

sections.heading: Notes
items: Use consultation paperwork and client interview to assess tolerance for trunk flexion
Omit abdominal machine for clients with orthopedic restrictions until medically cleared
For some with issues on this exercise dynamically, a conservative strategy is to perform a Timed Static Contraction (TSC):
Pin weight too heavy to lift with movement arm near midpoint
Lead client through progressive static effort
30 seconds @ 50% effort
30 seconds @ 75% effort
30 seconds @ 100% effort
Perform at least weekly for long-term strength gains and potential dynamic progression
Expect carryover benefit of approximately 15 degrees in either direction from held position
If TSC is not feasible, consider substituting with Torso Rotation to benefit abdominal musculature without trunk flexion
Machine’s resistance profile is heavier at the lower turnaround and lighter at the top
Contracted position may be used instinctively as a rest point by clients; avoid this by placing a selector pin in an upper stack pin hole to truncate end range (UT)
If truncation strategy is ever to be used, instructor must test it personally and document setup clearly in client chart

cards.title: Adduction – Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: Adductor Brevis (Inner Thigh) – Hip horizontal adduction
Adductor Longus (Inner Thigh) – Hip horizontal adduction
Adductor Magnus (Inner Thigh) – Hip horizontal adduction
Pectineus (Inner Thigh) – Hip horizontal adduction
Gracilis (Inner Thigh) – Hip horizontal adduction

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: Seat back typically standardized at position 6 or 7
Instructor must assist client with entry and exit; take full responsibility for safety during setup
Main setup consideration is establishing a conservative ROM for intro using custom gap for every subject
Clear main stack (and accessory stack if needed) before setting the gap
Ensure movement arms are far enough apart, then have the client take a seat
Begin bringing movement arms together and cue client to lift left leg into place, then right leg
Slowly allow movement arms apart, maintaining contact with leg/hand to avoid sudden movement
Ask client to indicate when a slight stretch is felt on the inner thigh
Set selector pin into desired main stack weight and record gap
Instructor should use judgment if client requests more stretch; assess risk/benefit

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Sit back, butt back, neutral head
Feet and ankles relaxed
Hands on handles for balance, not anchoring
Encourage relaxed upper body with optional abdominal contraction

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: Load Up
From lower turnaround, establish neutral head, hands on handles, and steady breathing
Gradually begin pressing knees together
Instructor observes closely; affirm with “good” or “mmm, hmm” when performed correctly
Concentric Phase / Upper Turnaround
Smoothly drive knees together into upper turnaround
Pause in the contracted position for about 1-2 seconds on first two reps, then 2–3 seconds from rep three onward
Instructor clicks at the exact moment the contraction duration ends
Eccentric Phase
Immediately after the click, cue “ease out, do not speed up”
Establish the expectation for the first lower turnaround during the eccentric: “touch and go,” “be continuous,” or “seamlessly change directions as the weights touch”
Always provide a cue on the first eccentric phase of the set
Lower Turnaround
Continuous movement at the bottom—“touch and go” without pausing
Maintain same controlled pace throughout
Execution
Continuous cadence with only a “brief but definite” pause in the contracted position (1-2 seconds for first two reps, 2–3 seconds from third rep on)
Do not rely solely on the word “squeeze”—teach the client HOW to contract
Example verbiage
“Continue to drive your knees together…keep breathing, lock it in place, [click], ease out…keep that pace.”
Only full reps are counted/recorded on chart
Set may continue after full ROM is lost if reps remain under strict control and client is advanced and/or tolerant of higher levels of intensity
Set continuation after concentric failure should be assessed with Studio Leader or MSF Corporate
For newer clients, a few full reps may be sufficient, specifically on Adduction; failure is not required in initial sessions
Encourage consistent pace while increasing effort as fatigue builds
Effort must rise to counter fatigue for mechanical tension to remain stimulative

sections.heading: Notes
items: Instructor must remain fully responsible for client safety during entry/exit
Entire movement arm setup must be under instructor control with clear and timely instruction
Always begin with a conservative stretch to avoid vulnerable positions
Gradual increases in stretch may be warranted over time if strength and tolerance improve
Increased ROM should only occur under instructor supervision and with Studio Leader
Cue clients to press through knees, even if knees do not directly contact the thigh pads
Referring to the knees simplifies instruction even though the femur is the acting lever
Special Populations / Conservative Approaches
Clients with hip replacements or related issues may not tolerate this movement pattern
Most conservative approach is to avoid the exercise, but strengthening may provide benefit
Alternative: Timed Static Contraction (TSC)
Use weight too heavy to lift and set movement arms at midpoint
Instruct static pressing against thigh pads in progressive intensity stages:
30 seconds @ 50% effort
30 seconds @ 75% effort
30 seconds @ 100% effort
TSC performed weekly over time builds strength and may allow eventual dynamic movement; expect ~15 degrees of ROM carryover in strength
Progression Considerations
Continuous Tension protocol typically starts with lighter weight, higher reps, and longer sets
Excessive time under load can lead to discomfort before stimulus is achieved
Over time, look to target perfect form with 6-second positive and 6-second negative reps
Aim for heavier weights that lead to failure in 10 or fewer reps when appropriate as this will act to minimize discomfort
If client demonstrates sufficient control, intensity may be progressed more quickly

cards.title: Biceps Curl – Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: Biceps Brachii (Biceps) – Elbow flexion

sections.heading: Synergists
items: Wrist Flexors (Forearms) – Wrist stabilizer

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: Seat height is the primary setup consideration
A gap (usually 1–2) is generally required for the introduction to ensure safety and assess tolerance at the lower turnaround
The Biceps Curl carries a higher potential risk due to loading at full extension; the gap reduces this risk
Seat height should correlate to subject’s height: taller subjects → lower seat, shorter subjects → higher seat
Seat too high → upper arm hovers above pad, only elbow makes contact
Seat too low → elbow doesn’t make contact, upper arm rests at bend of pad
Discomfort in triceps may indicate seat is set too low
Proper seat height should allow full contact of the upper arm with the pad while the chest remains upright against the chest pad
Align the machine’s axis with the elbow joint as closely as possible, though slight misalignment due to individual anatomy is acceptable
Elbow crease should point toward the ceiling, requiring slight external rotation of the humeri

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Use a chest-up posture, leaning into the chest pad
Arms should extend over the pad with elbow creases pointing upward
Instructor lifts the handles from resting position to remove slack; this is the lower turnaround and starting position
Subject grasps handles, palms up, equidistant from center
Instructor supports the movement arm with open hand and cues the subject: “The exercise will begin from this position”
Feet should be flat on the floor or on toes of shoes if shorter

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: LOAD UP
From lower turnaround: chest up, neutral head, relaxed face, breathing freely
Subject gradually applies pressure: elbows down into pad and simultaneous upward pull on handles keeping the wrists flat
Gradual load-up may require slight acceleration to maintain smoothness (same with every exercise)
Instructor quietly observes; positive reinforcement if appropriate
CONCENTRIC/UPPER TURN
Maintain smooth pace, chest up, head still, wrists flat
Flex elbows tightly to the maximum contraction point
Avoid over-pulling or flexing wrists, which risks unloading the muscle and bringing the arm too close to the face
Pause briefly at the contracted position: 1-2 seconds for first two reps, then 2–3 seconds on rep 3 and beyond
Provide actionable coaching cues during the squeeze phase (e.g. “tighten your elbow joint as hard as you can... keep breathing... [click], ease out”)
ECCENTRIC
After click, instruct subject to “ease out, do not speed up”
Cue first lower turnaround as “touch and go” or “seamlessly change directions”
Observe carefully to ensure subject maintains control at lower turnaround
Maintain chest up and elbows leveraged firmly into the pad
LOWER TURN
Lower turnaround is continuous with no pause; “touch and go”
Closely monitor for control to minimize risk at full extension
Reinforce elbow pressure into pad and posture control
INTENSITY
Set ends when subject can no longer achieve initial degree of elbow flexion with perfect form (i.e. concentric failure)
Only record full reps completed
Partial reps beyond midpoint may be used depending on subject experience and tolerance to intensity
Newer or deconditioned clients should not perform partials initially; focus on fewer full reps with perfect form
Effort must increase as set progresses to maintain pace with rising fatigue
Stimulative mechanical tension comes from increasing voluntary effort under fatigue

sections.heading: Notes
items: Instructor ‘clicks’ only after confirming full contraction and pause has occurred
Subject may mistakenly wait for click to initiate pause; instructor must control this by being assertive and timely
Gap of 1–2 is generally used at first; may be reduced or removed with stronger, more controlled subjects
Full range of motion is not inherently better; individual tolerance should guide range
Elbow should maintain some bend at lower turnaround even with full ROM
Isometric versions (Static Hold or Timed Static Contractions) may be appropriate for injuries such as tennis or golfer’s elbow or for those that cannot lift the 20 pound minimum
For isometrics, instructor assists into and out of position; refer to specific static hold protocol
Lighter weights in early learning may lead to longer sets; this will likely provide diminishing returns due to discomfort occurring prior to stimulus
Over time, look to progress to higher intensity with a more challenging load once form, tolerance, and understanding are established (e.g. 6-sec concentric/6-sec eccentric to failure in ≤10 reps)
Common compensations include lifting elbows off pad or flexing wrists; also likely to shrug in an exaggerated fashion; these must be corrected
Emphasize the goal: maximum muscle tension, not excessive machine movement
Instructor must consistently reinforce proper muscle recruitment and discourage movement compensations

cards.title: Cervical Extension – Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: Trapezius (Upper Back/Neck Extensors)
Semispinalis Muscle Group
Splenius Capitis
Longissimus Muscle Group
→ All contribute to Cervical Extension

sections.heading: Synergists
items: Erector Spinae – Spinal Extension / Anterior Pelvic Tilt
Multifidus – Spinal Stability
Quadratus Lumborum (QL) – Spinal Extension / Anterior Pelvic Tilt

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: 1. Seat Height
Taller clients → lower seat; shorter clients → higher seat
Seat height affects vertical alignment of the machine’s axis with the cervical spine (typically C3–C5)
2. Seat Depth
Most clients should sit mid-seat, not fully back, to ensure horizontal alignment with machine’s axis
Instructor must pull movement arm (head pad) back before client sits
3. Back Pad
Light contact with client’s mid-back — do not push them forward
4. Practical Alignment (Most Important)
Back of head must sit flush and securely in the recess of the head pad
Too low = pad rides up over head
Too high = pad misses base of skull
Any shifting during execution = potential misalignment → reposition while unloaded
No gap required for this movement; full ROM based on comfort is acceptable
5. Instructor Role
Control movement arm at all times during setup
Adjust client’s position to fit the head securely into the pad
Typical start weight = 20 lbs (lightest)

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Upright posture with chest up, slight chin elevation
Feet flat (or heels supported), hands on front handles, elbows in
Cue: “Sit tall…chin up/down…scoot forward” as needed
Instructor brings head pad to client’s head, assessing flush contact
Stand to the side of client to check alignment
Hand off the load only after confirming zero movement; say “That is yours”
If unstable, cue: “Push harder,” “Hold it still,” etc.

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: Eccentric (Lowering)
Cue: “Let the head come forward…maintain flush contact with the pad”
Ribcage may need to drop slightly to maintain smooth contact
Cue: “Go as far forward as is comfortable”
Seamless change of direction at bottom (no pause)
Helpful cues
“Push squarely into the pad”
“Keep your head in the path of the machine”
Concentric (Lifting)
Cue: “Lift your head/chin while arching your back and lifting your chest”
Encourage full extension of cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine
Cue ideas
“Follow it all the way, back and down”
“Head to butt, butt to head”
“Draw a rainbow with the top of your head”
Upper Turnaround
Pause only after maximal, safe extension has been achieved
Trainer clicks only after movement stops and full contraction is reached
DO NOT cue client to wait for the click to stop; click follows correct completion
Important
NEVER train to failure
Stop the set before technical failure
Prioritize control and safety over intensity
Progress conservatively and gradually over time
Notes & Cautions
The cervical spine is less conditioned to external load → greater injury risk
Emphasize rotary movement (not linear push/pull)
Remind: “Lift/lower the chin” or “Arc the head”
Avoid letting client push straight back or slide on pad
Instructor must perfect handoff technique
Ideal rep range: ≤8 reps, especially early in training
Isometric Option (Static Hold or Timed Static Contraction):
Safe alternative for injured or deconditioned clients
Position just beyond neutral with chin slightly elevated
Cue: “Push back and down into the pad”
Instructor loads and unloads weight; no motion should occur

cards.title: Chest Flye – Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: Pectoralis Major (Chest/Pecs): Shoulder horizontal adduction

sections.heading: Synergists
items: Anterior Deltoid (Shoulder): Shoulder horizontal adduction

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: Determine seat height based on subject height: taller subjects generally need a lower seat, shorter subjects a higher seat
Fine-tune seat height so upper arm (humerus) slopes down slightly from shoulder to elbow, or is at least level to the floor in starting position
Humeral head should be slightly above or level with elbow when hands are on handles
Subject’s head should align near the padded “work box” overhead when seated
Theoretical alignment: shoulders under machine’s axes of rotation (determined by back pad position)
Practical alignment takes priority: elbows must remain beyond and in contact with roller pads throughout entire ROM
For longer arms, set back pad further from roller pads; for shorter arms, set back pad closer to roller pads
Ensure roller pads do not hit the client during movement (back pad too far forward) or lose contact with the elbows (back pad too far back)
Consider both arm length and torso size to determine optimal back pad position
Adjust to create an appropriate gap at the lower turnaround for a conservative stretch
Ideal starting position: elbows slightly behind the midline of the torso (frontal plane) when viewed from the side
For subjects with shoulder issues, use a larger gap and reduce stretch to accommodate tolerance

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Chest up, butt back, feet on stool
Chin slightly tucked (neutral)
Arms behind roller pads, hands on handles

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: Load Up: From lower turnaround, maintain chest-up posture, neutral head position, arms in place, establish breathing, gradually drive forward through elbows
Instructor quietly observes; use cues like “mmm, hmm” or “yes, just like that” for positive feedback if performed properly
Concentric / Upper Turn: Client drives elbows together until roller pads make contact; maintain chest-up posture throughout
Hold contracted position for 1 second on initial reps or 2–3 seconds from third rep onward
Instructor clicks at end of desired pause/squeeze to begin eccentric
Eccentric: Immediately cue with “ease out, keep that pace” or equivalent

Lower Turnaround: Cue client with phrases like “touch and go,” “be continuous at the bottom,” “barely touch, barely start,” “seamlessly change direction as the weights touch,” or “soft touch, do not pause”
Lower turnaround must be continuous and controlled; avoid bottom pausing to adhere to Continuous Tension protocol
One continuous pace throughout set
Pause for ~1 second at contraction on first two reps, squeeze 2–3 seconds on subsequent reps
Avoid vague cues like “squeeze”; provide clear instruction on how to contract
Example verbiage

“Keep your chest up and gently bring those pads together… now keep breathing and continue to drive through your elbows, attempting to further dent those pads… keep still… [click], ease out… don’t speed up”
Maintain posture, head position, consistent pace, and continuous contact with arm pads
Only full reps reaching proper contraction are counted toward total rep number
If full ROM is no longer achievable but control remains, instructor may allow continuation of partial reps for stimulative tension
Decision to extend set beyond concentric failure is individual; consult studio Leader or MSF Corporate as needed
For new clients, completing a few full reps may be sufficient; failure is not required if discomfort, form degradation, or lack of readiness is evident
Effort must increase during the set to maintain consistent pace under increasing fatigue; this creates effective mechanical tension

sections.heading: Notes
items: Always point out overhead padded mechanism on entry/exit; say “watch your head” and gesture to ensure safety
If client has short arms and cannot reach handles without creating an upward humeral angle, have them grip the top of the roller pads instead
Chest Flye is effective for clients with wrist, hand, or elbow issues who still need chest stimulation
Works well as a chest-focused supplement and can be paired with:
Overhead Press in one routine
Chest Press in an alternating routine
Allows for twice-weekly chest stimulation without overloading arms or grip
During early stages of learning Continuous Tension protocol, client will likely use light weights and complete more reps
Excessive time under tension from high rep counts may lead to discomfort before reaching stimulative levels
Progress to heavier weights (~10 reps max) with controlled 6-second concentric and 6-second eccentric cadence once form is consistently demonstrated

cards.title: CP - Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: Pectoralis Major – Shoulder horizontal adduction
Triceps – Elbow extension
Anterior Deltoid – Shoulder horizontal adduction

sections.heading: Synergists
items: Erector Spinae – Spinal extension / anterior pelvic tilt
Lower Trapezius – Scapular stabilizer
Rotator Cuff – Shoulder stabilizers

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: Provide stool for all clients to support legs (knees should be higher than hips)
Provide stool for entry if needed and assist client in safely getting into position
Set seat height so upper arm is abducted 30–45° off body, with elbow ~90° or more
Ensure handle aligns with hands in this position
If seat is too high: elbows will be above hands
If seat is too low: elbows significantly below hands
Ideal: elbows slightly lower than hands on handles, forearms aligned with movement arm path (forearm will be angled/tracking slightly upward)
Place heel of palm on bend of handle for semi-pronated grip (thumbs slightly rotated upward)

Determine seat back position by ensuring full elbow extension (or just short of full ext) at upper turnaround without protraction; handles should fully converge; consider the effect of loading when assessing
Chest remains up and ribcage rigid through entire ROM
Assist handles back with client’s hands on handles to a conservative stretch to determine lower turnaround
For compromised shoulders: elbow stays forward of torso midline (less stretch)
For healthy shoulders: elbow can be just behind torso midline (more stretch)
Record the gap (lower turnaround) on chart
Account for compression of padding and flexing of movement arms under load when setting gap and seat back

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Chest up, hips back, chin tucked (neutral head), shoulders retracted
Upper arms abducted 30–45° (elbows out) and stay in that path for duration of set
Feet on stool with knees above hips for postural support and stability
Avoid dangling feet to minimize shifting and reduce discomfort
Hands placed at bend of handles; slight adjustments above or below bend if needed
Consider hand pads to reduce pressure
Begin movement from lower turnaround

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: Load Up
Maintain posture, neutral head, elbows out
“Establish breathing, gradually begin to apply pressure, pushing from chest”
Observe closely and silently after instruction
Provide brief positive feedback if appropriate (“perfect,” “yes, just like that”)
Concentric Phase
Arms converge until handles touch or nearly touch
Elbows fully straighten or just short of it at upper turnaround
‘Click’ given precisely at moment handles converge (or furthest reached in concentric)
Eccentric Phase
Cue immediately after click: “ease out…do not speed up”
No pause at upper turnaround (never on compound pushing movements)
Lower Turnaround
Always cue during first eccentric phase to define turnaround expectations
Use cues like “touch and go,” “be continuous at the bottom,” “soft touch, do not pause,” etc.
Maintain posture, head, pace, and consistent arm/elbow path

sections.heading: Notes
items: Explain gradual load-up if needed: describe ramping pressure or visual analogy of cracking weight stack
Gradual load-up may take 3–5 seconds before movement begins
No pause in chest press; emphasize exaggerated control at turnarounds
Ensure client fully reaches upper turnaround before clicking cue
Avoid premature clicks that confuse directional cueing
Seat height and back pad influenced by client’s height and arm length
Taller clients → lower seat; longer arms → back pad further back
Ensure elbow remains slightly lower than hand and follows the movement arm path
Movement arms travel out and up; hand and elbow should follow same trajectory
Emphasize joint stacking for optimal leverage and natural motion feel
With light loads during learning, expect more reps and longer time under tension
Be aware of discomfort vs. stimulation; avoid excessive duration that leads to intolerance
Progress to heavier loads and shorter sets (≤10 reps) with perfect form and faster reps (~6 sec up / 6 sec down) once client demonstrates control
Increase intensity appropriately as client learns Continuous Tension protocol
Encourage client to increase effort as fatigue builds to sustain pace
Reinforce that rising effort under fatigue is required for mechanical tension

cards.title: CR – Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: Rhomboids – Scapular Retraction/Adduction and Downward Rotation
Trapezius – Scapular Retraction/Adduction and Downward Rotation
Latissimus Dorsi – Shoulder Extension, Shoulder Adduction
Posterior Deltoid – Shoulder Horizontal Abduction, Shoulder Extension
Teres Major – Shoulder Extension
Biceps – Elbow Flexion, Forearm Supination
Brachioradialis – Elbow Flexion, Forearm Pronation, Supination

sections.heading: Synergists
items: Erector Spinae – Spinal Extension, Anterior Pelvic Tilt (chest-up posture)
Wrist Flexors – Wrist Flexion (grip support)

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: Set chest pad height based on client’s torso length and comfort; choose “up” or “down” position and note on chart
Adjust seat so handles are just within fingertip reach with arms fully extended and shoulders rounded forward slightly
Use standard gap of 2 on the weight stack unless otherwise determined with help of MSF Corporate. Match chest pad location up to the handles
Confirm movement arm mechanism will clear top of client’s head
Move chest pad back and increase weight stack gap if movement arm is too close
Use middle handle width setting by default (“M” on chart); choose narrow or wide settings based on body size or target emphasis
Align handle settings with training intention (narrower for lats, wider for upper back)—random variation compromises outcome

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Chest up, hips back, slight forward lean into chest pad
Ensure hips are not tucked under chest pad as this encourages leaning back
Client and trainer pull handles together just beyond midpoint for handoff
Ensure client can contribute to initial handle retrieval—leverage is poor for trainer alone
Trainer should adopt wide stance and use both bodyweight and correct grip for assist
Use one hand on bottom of arm and one on pronated handle when assisting
Cue client during load transfer with, “That is yours,” or similar language
Delay handoff if client cannot yet stabilize—cue “pull harder” or “increase your force”

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: Begin each set near the contracted (upper turnaround) position with trainer assist. Actual handoff should occur just beyond midpoint
Reinforce scapular retraction and upright posture during handoff to establish target muscle awareness
After controlled handoff, cue subject to “slowly begin to let the arms straighten”
Once arms are extended, cue to “continuously” or “immediately” begin the concentric phase
Encourage seamless turnarounds—avoid any pauses or hesitation at LT
Weights may or may not touch at the bottom; allow if it reinforces consistent ROM or protects valgus elbow
Upper turnaround is defined by full contraction: elbows pass torso or align at torso side (depending on row variation)
Discourage excessive backward pulling that shifts focus to non-target tissues
Click only after full ROM and controlled pause have been achieved
Be aware that clients may wait for the click to determine when to stop, but it must be earned by contraction and control
Use specific verbal cues: “Draw the shoulders back,” “Pull with shoulder blades,” “Drive your elbows back,” (upper back-biased) or “Pull elbows into your sides” (lat-biased)
Maintain chest-up posture, neutral head, and consistent arm path on both concentric and eccentric
Elbows must follow identical paths on both phases to ensure precise loading
Intensity
End set at point of concentric failure with perfect form (or sooner for new/intensity adverse clients)
Record only complete repetitions on chart
Consider use of partial reps beyond failure if client is experienced and capable
Evaluate tolerance and readiness before applying extended set techniques
New clients may achieve stimulus from full reps only—progress intensity gradually
Reinforce that effort must increase to maintain constant pace as fatigue rises
Educate clients on the concept of increasing effort as a response to fatigue
Stimulative mechanical tension is created by matching or exceeding effort demands

sections.heading: Notes
items: Ensure movement arm clears the client’s head during entry, exit, and execution
Use neutral grip handles as default—they are generally the most shoulder-friendly
Set up so client can assist during entry and can release handles independently after set
Narrow arm paths bias the lats; wider arm paths bias upper back (trapezius, rhomboids, rear delts)
Scapular motion should increase with upper back emphasis—encourage retraction and protraction
Be aware of valgus elbow conditions—adjust ROM or switch to pronated handles if discomfort occurs
Pronated grip requires wider arm path and further elbow drive for upper back emphasis
Adjust chest pad height based on spine length or unique needs (e.g., large abdomen or sternum sensitivity)
In early stages of Continuous Tension, expect higher reps due to lighter loads
Avoid excessively long time under tension if discomfort outweighs stimulus
Prioritize perfect form and gradually increase resistance and possibly the pace (6-second concentric/6-second eccentric, ≤10 reps/set)
Progress intensity only after demonstrating control and understanding of the movement

cards.title: LC – Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: Hamstrings – Knee Flexion
Gastrocnemius (Calf) – Knee Flexion

sections.heading: Synergists
items: Sartorius – Assists in Knee Flexion
Gracilis – Assists in Knee Flexion
Wrist Flexors – Gripping/Holding – anchoring into seat with arms

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: Set an initial gap of 1 or 2 on the weight stack as an introduction to the exercise (this will be determined by the Studio Leader and MSF Corporate). A gap of 3 or more may be required for knee injuries/issues
Move seat to rearmost position to allow maximum surface area
Subject sits with femurs cantilevered off front edge of seat and lower legs hanging freely
Patellas must not be under the roller pad; they should approximate or “crowd” the pad, with the top of tibia under the pad
Subject leans slightly forward, seat back is brought forward to just contact the lower back without pushing knees ahead of axis
Verify knees are aligned with axis of rotation
Subject exits the machine to allow for weight selection and proper loading
Use assist bar and trainer’s right knee to pull the movement arm down to mid-range, allowing subject to sweep legs in from the side
Lower the weight gently to establish starting position with clients legs extended and between pads
ALTERNATE LOADING: If the weight is too heavy to assist manually, use only the accessory stack initially, then select main stack weight after the subject is loaded
Adjust the calf pad to contact the lowest part of the back of the leg just above the achilles tendon so as not to contact the shoe

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Chest up, lay back against seat with head neutral and eyes forward
Hands firmly gripping handles, pulling up for leverage
Feet and ankles relaxed during setup and initial repetitions
Secure seat belt across hip crease and pull tight

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: Begin from lower turn with feet/ankles relaxed and pulling up on handles
Gradually build pressure by bending knees into roller pad to create force couple with the lower leg
Instructor gives cue to initiate load up; observe movement carefully
First concentric ends with a brief pause at maximal knee flexion; cue with “mmm…hmm” or “just like that” if properly controlled then [click]
After first concentric, cue “ease out and do not speed up”
Establish lower turnaround expectations: “touch and go,” “barely touch, barely start,” or “seamless change of direction”
Keep hips down by anchoring with hands if necessary
From third rep on, dorsiflex ankles to better leverage calves after the lower turn and during concentric
Cue: “keep the ankles relaxed during the turn… now pull the feet up to the knees”
At upper turn, cue: “keep ankles flexed, keep movement arm still, keep breathing, [click], relax ankles, THEN ease out”
Ensure no movement occurs during ankle relaxation
Maintain consistent pace with brief 1-2 second pauses on first two reps, and 2–3 second “squeeze” from third rep on
Teach HOW to squeeze with detailed cues such as: “pulling up on the handles, drive your knees into the pad, heels toward rear end, keep breathing, [click], relax ankles, ease out”
Maintain posture, neutral head, consistent arm leverage, and proper contact on roller pads
Movement should only occur at the knee joint; arms may engage more as leverage increases
Record only full reps; perform partial reps only if experienced and able to control beyond concentric failure
For new clients or those in discomfort, the set may end before loss of range of motion (i.e. concentric failure)
Encourage maintaining pace with increasing effort as fatigue builds
Educate that mechanical tension increases as voluntary effort overcomes increasing fatigue

sections.heading: Notes
items: Describe gradual pressure during load-up; use examples such as 20–40–60 lbs of pressure or “just enough to crack the stack”
Dorsiflexion is introduced after the first two reps to engage the gastrocnemius for added strength and deeper contraction
Ankles are relaxed during eccentric to isolate hamstrings
Toggling between dorsiflexion and relaxation improves control and enhances muscle awareness
Adjust intensity based on the client’s conditioning level; less intensity needed for beginners
Teach intensity progression through quality control and calm focus
Expect and address common discomforts or fears of cramps as often they are unfamiliar sensations, may not be true cramping
If full knee flexion is not achievable, redefine full range of motion for that client and document accordingly (e.g. limited ROM)
Consider using a hard end stop with the extra selector pin at the subject’s contracted position to improve consistency and provide a point to pull into
Document pin placement using the number of empty holes between the top of the stack and the selector pin (i.e. gap for the upper turn)
Full contraction is not necessary for benefit but may help with establishing a neuromuscular connection
Continuous Tension protocol will likely start with lighter weights and higher reps
Lighter loads may lead to discomfort before stimulus; strive for faster tempo over time (6 sec concentric, 6 sec eccentric) with heavier loads once control is established
Adjust progression based on the client’s demonstrated control and tolerance. Progress slowly for those that warrant it

cards.title: LE – Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: Quadriceps (Thighs) – Knee extension: all four heads of the quadriceps active, especially the Rectus Femoris which is not stimulated during pressing patterns

sections.heading: Synergists
items: Brachioradialis (Forearms) – anchoring into seat with arms
Wrist Flexors (Forearms) – gripping/holding for anchoring

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: LE will typically have a gap of 2 as an introduction to the exercise
Move the seat back to the rearmost position to maximize seat surface
With tibia pad in the bottom position, have subject sit with legs hanging off at the knee; align knee joint with machine’s axis of rotation
Subject should lean forward slightly while seat back is brought forward to make contact with pelvis without pushing them forward beyond axis
Subject should sit fully back into the seat; ensure knee remains aligned with axis and there is no excessive pressure behind the knee
Once the position is finalized, have subject exit for proper loading
Standard gap of 2 in most cases due to significant knee flexion; confirm specifics with MSF Corporate during installation (gap may be larger for knee issues)
Select appropriate weight and gap
Use assist bar to move tibia pad; subject enters seat rear-first and sweeps legs behind tibia pad
Lower tibia pad onto subject’s shins, ensure contact just above the top of the foot
Alternative Loading Method
If weight is too heavy to move with assist bar, load desired weight on accessory stack and remove main stack pin
Move tibia pad out of way, client enters seat, and trainer lowers movement arm into place
Trainer may need to counter the passive resistance of subject’s legs to position movement arm at the required gap
Trainer selects appropriate main stack weight and gap after securing client
Secure seatbelt in subject’s hip crease; belt should not restrict femurs
Trainer may need to request the other end of the seat belt from the subject

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Chest up, back laid against the seat, head upright and neutral
Hands pulling up on handles for leverage, breathe freely
Face, jaw, feet, and ankles relaxed throughout the set

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: Begin from lower turn with neutral head, relaxed feet and ankles, pulling up on handles
Establish breathing and gradually apply pressure into tibia pad to initiate knee extension
Instructor should provide feedback after gradual load up (“mmm, hmm” or “yes, just like that”)
Subject moves to full knee extension; brief pause or squeeze at upper turn with optional “click”
After the first concentric, cue “ease out and do not speed up”
During first eccentric, cue lower turnaround: “touch and go,” “be continuous,” or “barely touch, barely start”
Maintain hips down using leverage from handles
Use continuous pace with “brief but definite” pause of 1 second in contracted position for first two reps, progressing to 2–3 second squeeze from third rep on
Provide clear instruction for HOW to perform squeeze (e.g. “pull up on handles, fully straighten knees, keep breathing, keep still, [click], ease out”)
Maintain posture, head position, pace, and alignment; movement occurs only at the knee
Only full reps reaching full extension count toward recorded total
Instructor may allow continuation after concentric failure if partial reps are controlled and client is experienced/comfortable with higher intensity
Avoid pushing new clients to failure; a few full ROM reps may suffice for introduction for those that do not have resistance training experience
Teach effort progression; effort must increase with fatigue to maintain pace and tension

sections.heading: Notes
items: Explain “gradual” to the client: e.g. “20 pounds… 40 pounds… find just enough force to crack the stack”
Emphasize 3–5 second gradual load-up phase
Provide imagery like “denting the shin pads” to reinforce progressive pressure
Instruct subject to relax feet and ankles to prevent dorsiflexion, which can inhibit quadriceps contraction due to calf tension
Tailor intensity based on individual conditioning; newer clients require lower intensity for an effective stimulus and should be progressed slowly
Encourage control and technique before intensity; demonstrate care and attention to their experience
If client appears unable to fully straighten knees, it may be helpful to assess joint capability with a no-load demonstration (knee extension without movement arm)
Use anchoring and verbal cues (“straighten further”) to determine if limitation is structural or behavioral
If structurally limited, note “limited ROM” or “limit ext” on chart for consistency
Consider using a hard end stop (pin placed above weight stack) for those unable to reach full extension; this gives feedback on ROM and allows trainer to track
Document position of upper selector pin if used (count empty holes-gap)
Hard end stop encourages consistency, provides a cue for effort, and offers a defined termination point
Full knee extension is not required for effective stimulation; contraction helps motor unit recruitment and kinesthetic awareness
Be prepared to avoid or modify exercise for those with knee issues
Most conservative option: Timed Static Contraction (TSC) – position movement arm mid-range, pin a heavy weight that cannot be lifted, cue subject through increasing effort:
50% for 30 sec
75% for 30 sec
100% for final 30 sec (90 sec total)
Static has reported ~15 degrees carryover in either direction
TSC can improve strength and eventually allow dynamic use
Another conservative alternative: Static Hold (SH) – load is held against end stop
Select load and insert upper selector pin to stop concentric movement
Assist client into and out of hold position
Initial duration: 30–45 sec; progress to 120 sec max
Once 120 sec is achieved, increase weight and reduce time to progress intensity
Continuous Tension protocol: lighter weight allows more reps and longer duration
Be cautious with prolonged light sets that may lead to discomfort before stimulus
Strive for heavier weight over time and controlled 6/6 tempo leading to failure in ≤10 reps - this would be ideal but not all clients will tolerate this load
Progress intensity as soon as client demonstrates control and understanding

cards.title: LP – Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: Quadriceps – Knee Extension
Gluteus Maximus – Hip Extension

sections.heading: Synergists
items: Hamstrings
Gastrocnemius
Soleus
Adductor Magnus

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: Determine seat back position: default to P2 for most. Consider P3 for larger subjects or limited hip flexion tolerance. P3 may increase shoulder pad pressure and hip rise risk.
Set shoulder pads to touch the tops of shoulders when subject is reclined.
Pin accessory stack at 18 lbs. Leave main stack clear; instructor holds selector pin.
Instructor advances footplate forward to reachable distance for client’s leg length.
Position feet hip-width apart on footplate to align ankles, knees, and hips (“stacked”). Feet should be parallel.
Use wider stance and slight toe-out for subjects with larger frames or limited external rotation. Ensure knees track in line with feet.
Instructor carefully releases footplate over client’s control (knees still slightly bent with feet on footplate). Combined 38 lbs of pressure from footplate helps client secure foot position.
Adjust seat so footplate abuts end stop just before full knee extension. Move seat a couple settings closer to account for compression under load (first-time setup only).
Bring footplate back to desired starting (lower turnaround) position. Instructor may need to assist pulling back on footplate due to limited hip flexion (first-time setup only).
Pin main weight stack when footplate is at desired position. Client may pin weight if easier; otherwise, instructor should do so (initial setup only).
Account for additional spacing created under load from padding compression and arm flex.

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Lay back with head forward or supported by seat back.
Hands on either set of handles.
Face relaxed, jaw relaxed, breathing freely.

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: Load Up
From lower turnaround, maintain neutral head (“chin down”), establish breathing, then gradually apply pressure through the footplate.
Instructor provides “gradual load up” cue and observes carefully. Positive feedback optional if done correctly.
Concentric
Smooth pace to upper turnaround (end stop). ‘Click’ at the moment the end stop is reached or effort limit. No pause.
Eccentric
Keep upper turn continuous with timing of ‘click’ and cue “ease out…do not speed up” or “be continuous…keep that pace”
Proactively cue during first eccentric: “touch and go,” “be continuous at the bottom,” “barely touch, barely start,” or “seamlessly change direction.” No pause
Lower Turnaround
Be continuous/seamless, make sure to bottom out but do not unload, avoid Val Salva, do not fire out of the bottom
Execution Notes
Keep hips down; avoid pelvis roll or tailbone lift
Maintain continuous pace until concentric failure—no pause at any point.
Maintain posture, head position, pace, and knee path throughout.
Knees must track consistently in both directions to keep joints stacked and loading.
As fatigue increases, effort must increase to maintain pace and stimulate tension.

sections.heading: Notes
items: May need to explain “gradual” load-up: e.g., “build just enough pressure to move stack (101 lbs pressure to lift 100 lbs). May take 3–5 seconds.”
No pause at any point. Emphasize control at direction changes (“drag out the turn” or “almost pause but do not”).
If feet slide or torso shifts up seat back, ensure knees do not fully extend. Cue appropriately and click if needed. Adjust settings for next set if necessary.
Higher foot position (and higher seat back P2) = decreased knee flexion, increased hip flexion → more glute biased.
Lower foot position (and lower seat back P3) = increased knee flexion → more quad biased. Both muscle groups contribute regardless.
Tailor intensity to client’s experience. Newer/deconditioned clients require less intensity. Start light, teach control, progress gradually.

Newer clients may use lighter weights and perform more reps. Excess duration may cause discomfort before stimulation. Ideally we prefer perfect reps (6s up / 6s down) with heavier load leading to failure in ≤10 reps once control is established.
Some clients won’t “feel” their glutes despite correct setup. Glutes still active in movement.
Upright seat increases hip/spinal flexion; if discomfort occurs, increase gap (shallower lower turnaround) even if it reduces glute emphasis.
Avoid pairing LP with Lumbar if client has sensitive lower back. If included in same workout, place several exercises between them to allow lumbar “pump” to subside.
Consider doing ABD prior to LP to pre-fatigue glutes and improve sensation of glute engagement.

cards.title: Lumbar – Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: Erector Spinae (Spinal Erectors/Spinal Extensors) – Spinal Extension/Anterior Pelvic Tilt
Multifidus – Spinal Extension/Spinal Stability
Quadratus Lumborum (QL’s) – Spinal Extension/Anterior Pelvic Tilt

sections.heading: Synergists
items: Gluteus Maximus – Stabilizer
Latissimus Dorsi – Spinal Extension
Trapezius – Stabilizer, Scapular Retraction/Adduction and Downward Rotation

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: If accessory weight stack will be used, it must be set prior to client sitting
Move carriage all the way back and place pin in main stack to lock movement arm
Determine seat pad height by
Practical Alignment - look for the back pad to land on as much of the shoulder blade area as possible
Theoretical Alignment - use iliac crest alignment with top of the roller pad
Monitor top-heaviness that may add leverage and reduce effectiveness (i.e. shoulder blades above back pad) - seat might be too high
Raise and move femur restraint to clear space for footplate adjustment
Position footplate so knee joint is slightly higher than hip joint, creating a downward femur slope
Place seatbelt across hip crease after feet are on footplate and femur restraint is in place
Ensure femur restraint pads straddle patella evenly; upper pad on femur, lower on tibia
Pads should be snug with slight wiggle room and angle congruent with femur and tibia
If pads are not congruent to knee, adjust foot placement on footplate; raise foot if knee angle is too severe
Adjust footplate as needed after foot repositioning
Secure femur restraint snugly after all lower body alignment is complete
Establish lower turnaround by removing main stack pin and carefully pulling movement arm and subject forward
Adjust lower turnaround conservatively based on client size and consider any history of low back issues
Most benefits are derived from the extension phase; avoid deep flexion under load
Recheck and tighten femur pads after setting lower turnaround as subject will have likely slid back some

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Cue: “Chin tucked, chest up, establish your breathing and gradually begin to build pressure into the back pad by lifting the ribcage”
Prevent lifting the head and breath hold during effort initiation
Deliver cue slowly and clearly for client processing and implementation

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: Load Up
Cue gradual pressure into back pad
Observe quietly and reinforce with “perfect” or “yes, just like that” if appropriate
Check for overly emphasized leg drive, especially if knees are not higher than hips
Concentric
Cue: “Chest up, back arched…” or “Lift your chest and arch your back”
Use descriptive language to guide the process of spinal extension
Avoid relying solely on potentially confusing terms like “extend your spine” or “squeeze”
Upper Turn
Observe range and tolerance at end stop
Confirm full range achieved if tolerable. Watch the stopper abutt the frame
Pause briefly at upper turnaround for 1-2 seconds; beginning with rep 3, implement 2–3 second squeeze
Cue: “Keep arching, keep breathing, [click], ease out”
Always instruct how to squeeze, do not just say “squeeze”
Eccentric
Click at the end of the squeeze duration
Cue: “Ease out, and do not speed up” or similar
Use first eccentric of every exercise to set expectations for lower turn
Lower Turn
Cue for lower turnaround: “Touch and go,” “be continuous at the bottom,” “barely touch, barely start,” “seamlessly change direction,” or “soft touch, do not pause”
As with all instruction, timing is critical; the cue needs to come before the turn
Overall Execution Notes
Never take lumbar extension to failure; extra precaution with new subjects or those with low back issues
Posture and Path are essentially controlled due to restraints, which makes this movement easier to learn
Reinforce reminders for head position and spinal extension
Emphasize maintaining a consistent and controlled pace
Client must increase effort across set as fatigue increases
Ensure every rep is completed with exacting control

sections.heading: Notes
items: Screen all clients for contraindications and movement limitations during consultation (review intake/demographics packet and discuss)
Avoid lumbar extension altogether for those with known orthopedic issues unless medically cleared
Consider a conservative starting point using Timed Static Contraction (TSC):
Pin heavy weight to prevent movement - this is a static variation
Position movement arm just beyond midpoint of ROM (slightly biased toward upper turnaround)
Cue static effort progression: 30 seconds @ 50%, 30 seconds @ 75%, 30 seconds @ 100%;  NOTE: may need to introduce even more conservatively with shorter duration (15 seconds vs. 30 at each level)
Perform at least weekly for several months for strength improvements
TSC has a reported ~15° carryover range; may enable future dynamic use
Variability in setup can impact performance (e.g., footplate, femur restraint, seatbelt tension)
Maintain setup consistency and document all “fine tuning” adjustments
If client reports discomfort from the roller pad
Consider that it may be from the client’s waistline of pants or belt
Evaluate footplate height; knees too high may increase pressure
Raise or lower seat to adjust roller contact point as needed
Record all adjustments for consistency in future sessions

cards.title: OH - Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: Anterior Deltoid – Shoulder Abduction, Shoulder Flexion
Middle Deltoid – Shoulder Abduction, Shoulder Flexion
Triceps – Elbow Extension
Pectoralis Major – Assists in Shoulder Flexion

sections.heading: Synergists
items: Rectus Abdominis – Posterior Pelvic Tilt (PPT)
Subscapularis – Shoulder Stabilizer
Posterior Deltoid – Shoulder Stabilizer
Trapezius – Scapular Rotation and Stabilizer (Scapulohumeral Rhythm)

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: Evaluate if subject needs a stool for entry and/or leg support
Confirm seat height using the standard gap of 2 on the weight stack
Seat height is correct if subject’s arms hang naturally at the sides then with just an elbow bend, the hands land near the ends of the handles
For compromised shoulder joints, consider lowering seat and/or increasing gap to reduce ROM
Ensure subject uses a neutral grip, with hands near bottom of the handles
Note that the handles are angled downward in the starting position and the forearm is perpendicular to the handle. This will ensure the proper arm path as the movement arm will follow an arc
Instruct subject to maintain a posterior pelvic tilt (PPT) with abdominal contraction
Account for pad compression and arm flex under load—adjust as needed

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Confirm PPT and explain its purpose: abdominal engagement and lumbar safety
Ensure head is in neutral position, chin slightly tucked, gaze downward
Hands near ends of handles, palms facing in; hand pads optional
Upper arms should be in the scapular plane (30°–40° anterior to frontal plane)
Scapulae should remain free—not forced into retraction or protraction
Feet must rest firmly on a support stool—no leg dangling
Movement should begin from lower turnaround position

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: Confirm starting posture: hips back, feet supported, PPT active, neutral head, scapular plane alignment
Cue a gradual load-up through palms—emphasize building pressure over 3–5 seconds
Provide initial observational feedback—reinforce proper beginning technique
Confirm force vector is perpendicular to angled handle (requires slight forward push)
Maintain consistent elbow path both concentrically and eccentrically
Ensure full arm extension at top—some natural scapular elevation is expected
Instruct to continue full ROM before clicking at upper turnaround—click timing is critical
Immediately post-click, cue: “Ease out, do not speed up”
Establish first eccentric expectation: “Touch and go,” “Be continuous,” or “Do not pause”
Confirm smooth, continuous pace—no stopping at turnarounds
Reinforce consistent posture, head position, pace, and arm path
Monitor and cue increased effort to match rising fatigue—stimulative tension is effort-dependent

sections.heading: Notes
items: Use analogies to explain gradual load-up (e.g., finding 101 lbs to crack a 100 lb stack)
Emphasize continuous effort—no pause, but slow transitions at turnarounds
Ensure full elbow extension before cueing upper turnaround click
Instructors should not cue the click prematurely—this can shorten ROM and create confusion
Adjust seat height and gap based on subject height and arm length
If subject experiences discomfort in upper range, limit ROM and use a selector pin to establish a consistent end range
During early stages of Continuous Tension learning, expect higher reps due to lighter load
Avoid excessive time under tension if it becomes more uncomfortable than stimulative
Progress to “faster” reps (6s up / 6s down) and heavier load targeting failure in ≤10 reps once control is established

cards.title: Pd - Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: Latissimus Dorsi (Shoulder Extension, Sagittal Plane, Supinated)
Teres Major, Posterior Deltoid, and Biceps (Elbow Flexion, Supination)

sections.heading: Synergists
items: Rhomboids (Scapular Downward Rotation)
Lower Trapezius (Scapular Depression)
Pectoralis Major and Triceps (Shoulder Extension)
Erector Spinae and Rectus Abdominis (Spinal/Pelvic Position)
Wrist Flexors - gripping

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: Provide stool if client requires assistance for entry or foot support
Handles in supinated position so the ends face in toward each other and slightly forward (one notch toward neutral)
Confirm subject is seated behind the vertical path of the handles (upper arm’s length)
Use back pad setting of 2 or 3 for most; 1 for larger subjects needing deeper seat placement
Avoid using seat positions 1-4 as that tends to be too high for shorter, more deconditioned clients to safely reach
As a result, using only seat positions 5-9 will require a larger gap of the weight stack
With subject seated bring handles down to them so that there is still a slight bend in the elbow and pin the weight stack and thus setting the gap
Ensure weight stack does not bottom out too soon; the subject’s arm should almost but not quite straighten at the lower turn (i.e. there should still be a slight bend in the elbow at the lower turn)
Grip should be shoulder-width or narrower to achieve narrow arm path for optimal lat engagement

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Cue chest up, hips back, chin slightly tucked, upper back in contact with seat back
Secure seat belt tightly
Provide stool option if legs are unsupported/uncomfortable or entry is difficult
Assist client in pulling handles toward contracted position near eye level
Perform controlled handoff using verbal cue (e.g., “that is yours”)
Confirm client establishes control before beginning eccentric
If movement occurs during handoff, cue “increase your force” or “pull harder”

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: Begin with handles near eye level using trainer assistance
Cue “slowly begin to let the arms straighten” for first eccentric
Once arms almost straighten, the weights should lightly touch, instruct immediate and controlled bending of the elbows (lower turnaround)
Weights usually touch at lower turnaround unless intentionally permitted to fully straighten without weights touching for purposes of a stretch
Full contraction occurs when elbows are pulled into the sides of the rib cage, not beyond the rib cage (upper turnaround), wrists should remain flat
Optional variation: cue abdominal contraction for added engagement at upper turnaround
Do not allow subject to lean forward or elbows to move behind torso during contracted abdomen variation
Ensure client does not over-pull or excessively flex wrists in an attempt to keep moving until the “click”
Click only after observing control and full ROM at upper turnaround with brief pause in contracted position
Cue examples: “Drive elbows into the sides of your ribcage… there… [click] ease out”
Maintain posture, head position, consistent pace, and arm path throughout set
Intensity
End set at true concentric failure with perfect form
Record only full, controlled reps achieved
Allow for partial reps beyond midpoint only with experienced clients demonstrating control and competency under duress
Avoid partials for newer or deconditioned clients; focus on consistent, full ROM
Emphasize progressive effort with perfect form throughout the set to overcome accumulating fatigue
Reinforce that effort must increase to maintain pace and produce meaningful stimulus

sections.heading: Notes
items: Torso Arm setup uses neutral grip and frontal plane movement (as opposed to sagittal plane with supinated grip)
Pulldown biases thoracic/lumbar divisions; Torso Arm biases iliac division of lats

Use Torso Arm for subjects that cannot tolerate supinated pattern. This may be for any number of reasons including hand/wrist issues, shoulder pain, elbow valgus, etc. Sometimes just making a slight modification can make for a more tolerable outcome. Torso Arm may also be a good form of variation for a more advanced client that has been with us for years.
Do not restrict natural scapular movement unless excessive shrugging is observed. The scapulae should naturally draw down with the arms
Prioritize stabilization of head and ribcage over scapular positioning
Handles should be reachable for assisted start and self-managed finish
Address valgus elbow issues with ROM modifications, pushing movement first, or grip variation
Avoid prolonged light-load sets in early stages; increase load and reduce time once control is evident
Ideal early progression: heavier load, 6–10 reps with 6-second tempo on both concentric and eccentric
This will be highly individual and some clients will need to stay with a lighter weight for higher reps even though it is not ideal

cards.title: PO – Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: Latissimus Dorsi (Lats) – Shoulder Extension

sections.heading: Synergists
items: Teres Major (Upper Back) – Shoulder Extension
Posterior Deltoid (Rear Delt) – Shoulder Extension
Rhomboids (Upper Back) – Scapular Downward Rotation with Adduction
Trapezius (Upper Back) – Scapular Adduction with Depression
Pectoralis Major (Chest) – Shoulder Extension
Triceps Brachii (Long Head) – Shoulder Extension
Rectus Abdominis – Thorax Stabilizer

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: Seat back has two positions: most clients will use the "up and back" position; smaller clients may use "down and forward"
Start with seat height based on subject height: taller = lower seat, shorter = higher seat
Align machine’s axis of rotation slightly above subject’s shoulder joint when seated with arms at sides
Expect shoulder joint to move during the exercise; alignment should reflect “average” midpoint of this excursion

Arm pad setting: choose Wide (W), Middle (M), or Narrow (N) based on torso width; most clients will likely use Middle; pads should be as narrow as possible to accommodate a narrow arm path into sides of torso
Elbows should land at least halfway down the arm pads and maintain a 90-degree angle throughout movement
Care must be given to bringing movement arm and arm pads down over the client; client may have to maneuver one arm at a time through pads
Standard lower turnaround gap is 6; always evaluate range of motion individually for safety
Reassess ROM if the instructor anticipates excessive range during first eccentric
Adjust settings if elbows slide or bend/straighten beyond 90 degrees during motion; this is the practical alignment requirement

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Establish a posterior pelvic tilt (PPT) to contract abdomen and create a rounded back posture
Avoid chest-up, arched-back posture and avoid pushing down with the hands on the movement arm
Pull movement arm over client with care, maneuvering arms between pads
Grab movement arm further from the axis for leverage during assist
Perform handoff with verbal cue (e.g. “driving back through your elbow, tighten your abdomen, that…is…yours”)
Ensure client establishes stillness and control before starting eccentric
Do not release full weight during handoff until client can maintain control
Cue increased force if movement occurs during handoff

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: Exercise begins in the contracted position (upper turnaround) with instructor assist
Use PPT and elbow-driven effort to reinforce desired muscular feeling
Cue client to “slowly begin to allow the movement arm to rise…keeping the pressure through the elbows” during first eccentric
Before lower turnaround, cue client to “continuously,” “seamlessly,” or “immediately” reverse direction by tightening abdomen and driving through elbows
Clarify that “immediate” does not mean “sudden”
Upper turnaround occurs when elbows are fully drawn into the sides and midsection is tightened
Instruct against pushing arm further just to lift the stack higher; emphasize muscular objective…elbows in, abdomen tight
Trainer clicks only after confirming full ROM and control in contracted position
Clients often anticipate a click to signal when to stop, but it must come after they stop
Trainer must assertively control timing and prevent client from overshooting ROM
Cue concentric movement with “draw the elbows down into the ribs”
Note: posture changes between phases – ribcage inevitably rises (anterior pelvic tilt) during eccentric and lowers (PPT) during concentric
Intensity
Set ends when subject reaches concentric failure with perfect form
Only full reps are recorded on the chart
Partial reps beyond midpoint may be included when form is excellent and client is sufficiently experienced and comfortable with higher intensities
Newer or deconditioned clients should focus on full reps to moderate fatigue
Always progress client’s understanding of effort and intensity across sessions
Effort must voluntarily increase to counteract fatigue and maintain pace, this is how to generate mechanical tension

sections.heading: Notes
items: Standard lower turnaround gap of 6 is generally conservative; confirm gap setting for each machine individually with Studio Leader and MSF Corp
Use of a selector pin near the upper turnaround can provide a concentric end stop
Static Hold or Timed Static Contraction versions of this exercise may be used for safety or instructional purposes
Pullover engages nearly all upper body muscles and is among the most demanding exercises in the studio when properly loaded and performed
During early sessions, lighter weights often allow for more reps and longer time under load, which is necessary for learning
Be cautious that prolonged sets with light weight do not lead to intolerable discomfort before adequate stimulus as subject progresses
Strive for perfect form using “faster” tempo (6 sec concentric, 6 sec eccentric) with heavier weights targeting failure in ≤10 reps
Increase intensity progressively once client demonstrates consistent control and understanding

cards.title: Seated Dip – Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: Pectoralis Major (Costal and Sternal Heads): Shoulder flexion from hyperextension, horizontal adduction
Triceps: Elbow extension
Anterior Deltoid: Shoulder flexion

sections.heading: Synergists
items: Erector Spinae: Spinal extension, anterior pelvic tilt (chest-up posture)
Lower Trapezius: Scapular stabilization
Serratus Anterior: Scapular depression and protraction
Latissimus Dorsi: Assists in shoulder flexion from hyperextension to anatomical position
Rotator Cuff: Shoulder stabilization

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: Most clients will require a stool to support the legs due to high seat position; some may also need a stool for entry
Seat height determines both the starting position and the intersection of hands with movement arms, affecting shoulder/elbow angles (lower turnaround)
Shorter clients will need a lower seat to more safely enter/exit the machine. In this case, there will likely be a gap to bring the handles down lower
Aim for upper arms abducted 45–60 degrees; elbows bent ~90° or more based on mobility

Humerus/elbow will likely be behind torso in starting position depending on seat and back pad setting; this tends to be a more shoulder friendly movement pattern than a Chest Press and can therefore allow more ROM at LT
Hands should be placed more forward on handles in starting position; establish consistent placement for all clients
Allow client to choose either neutral or pronated grip; pronated grip involves “capping” the ends of the handles; most seem to prefer pronated
Use Fat Gripz to distribute pressure and improve comfort; subject pushes through heel of palm rather than gripping
Favor a higher seat setting for safety to avoid excessive stretch of shoulder capsule and hyperflexion of elbows for those with shoulder issues
Adjust seat depth based on body size: smaller subjects may sit more forward, larger subjects more back; most will not use entire seat
If hands slip forward, adjust by moving forward in seat or repositioning hands slightly back on handles; consider hand pads
Set back pad angle and lower to meet mid/upper back to provide leverage; this promotes forward lean and will act to increase stretch at chest and shoulders
Adjustments may be necessary post-loading due to compression of padding and changes in spacing

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Raise seat back to allow proper entry into seat
Fasten seat belt tightly to counter upward force from movement
Once belted, lower seat back to desired setting (see above)
Set posture: chest up, hips back, head neutral (downward gaze due to forward lean), shoulders retracted, hands on handles
Upper arms abducted 45–60 degrees; elbows bent 90° or more
