Feet must contact a stool for stability and comfort; ball of the foot at least
Hands placed at/near end of movement arm (preferably Fat Gripz); choose neutral or pronated grip
Begin movement at lower turnaround; no gap necessary on this machine

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: Start from lower turnaround with rigid posture: chest up, shoulders retracted, chin tucked, upper arms abducted
Instruct gradual pressure through heel of palm while  breathing
Observe quietly at the beginning of the load-up; offer simple positive reinforcement if correctly executed
Ensure subject is leveraging off back pad
Movement arms travel down as subject attempts to
Straighten arms fully
Protract shoulder blades
Contract abdominals
These actions should occur synergistically to complete the upper turnaround
Instructor must watch for full contraction before clicking to indicate upper turnaround
Emphasize that clicking occurs only after movement stalls, not when handles are pushed as low as possible
Reinforce the goal is to fully contract—not just move handles further
Sample verbiage
“Drive your arms straight, and tighten down hard on the abdomen, keep breathing, [click], ease out”
“Keep straightening, keep breathing, round your back hard into the back pad, [click], ease out”
After first concentric and click, establish expectation for lower turnaround:
“Touch and go” / “Be continuous” / “Do not pause” / “Barely touch, barely start”
Maintain continuous pace throughout the set, with brief pause only as needed to ensure full contraction
Continue cycle until concentric movement stalls (muscular failure)
Maintain posture, head position, and consistent elbow tracking throughout (path)
Effort must increase to match rising fatigue in order to maintain pace and produce stimulative tension

sections.heading: Notes
items: Explain gradual load-up to client if needed
“20 lbs of pressure, 40 lbs, 60 lbs…” or “Pretend there's 100 lbs, find 101 lbs of pressure”
Load-up may take 3–5 seconds before movement occurs
No pause allowed during Seated Dip—movement must remain continuous
Emphasize controlled changes of direction: “drag out the turn” or “almost pause but don’t”
Ensure subject reaches full contraction before clicking for direction change
In early stages of learning MSF protocol with lighter weight, client may perform higher reps which will likely create discomfort well before stimulative reps
Over time, ideally progress to heavier loads (leading to failure ≤10 reps) once subject demonstrates control and acceptance of intensity
Form and understanding should guide intensity progression, not just tolerance to discomfort

cards.title: Simple Row – Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: Posterior Deltoid (Rear Delt): Shoulder horizontal abduction
Rhomboids (Upper Back): Scapular retraction/adduction and downward rotation
Trapezius (Upper Back): Scapular retraction/adduction and downward rotation

sections.heading: Synergists
items: Infraspinatus (Rotator Cuff): Shoulder horizontal abduction
Erector Spinae (Spinal Erectors): Stabilizers, spinal extension/anterior pelvic tilt (chest-up posture)

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: Determine seat height based on subject height: taller subjects likely need a lower seat, shorter subjects a higher seat
Fine-tune seat height so upper arm slopes down slightly (shoulder higher than elbow)
Subject’s head should be near the overhead padded “work box” when seated
For the chest pad, the theoretical alignment would have shoulders directly under axes of rotation
Practical alignment takes priority: elbow should land in at least the middle of the concave arm pads, and pads must remain flush through movement
Adjust chest pad based on arm length: longer arms = chest pad further from arm pads; shorter arms = chest pad in closer
Determine final chest pad setting based on interplay of arm length and torso size to ensure arm pads remain flush throughout
May require a gap for subjects with a wider frame; in some cases, the wider subject will need assistance for entry/exit by pulling movement arms apart
Adjust vertical handle height for longer arms to ensure elbows align with center of arm pads; hands do not hang from handle but rather wedge against them to create force couple with elbow
If external rotation is limited, advise client to “cap” the ends of the handles with palms facing themselves for comfort

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Chest up, hips close to chest pad so abdomen is against the pad
Head neutral, arms inside pads, hands on handles
Ensure abdomen contacts chest pad to allow ribcage lift and facilitate both thoracic extension and scapular retraction
Begin at lower turnaround with emphasized chest-up posture
Feet on floor; for shorter legs/higher seats, feet back on toe of shoe

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: Load Up: From lower turnaround, chest up, neutral head, arms in place, establish breathing, gradually apply pressure by driving out through elbows
After instruction, trainer quietly observes load up; offer affirmation if done correctly (e.g., “perfect” or “yes, just like that”)
Concentric / Upper Turn: Subject lifts chest and draws shoulder blades together until full contraction is achieved
Instructor clicks once desired duration in contracted position is reached
Eccentric: Immediately follow click with cue “ease out” or “do not speed up”
Lower Turnaround: Cue with “touch and go,” “be continuous,” or “seamlessly change directions”
Maintain chest-up posture using abdomen to leverage off chest pad
Execute at a continuous pace with a brief pause (~1 second) on first two reps and a 2–3 second squeeze from third rep onward
Avoid vague cues like “squeeze”—instead give actionable instructions on HOW to contract
Example verbiage
“Leveraging off your abdomen, lift your chest and draw your shoulder blades together as hard as you can… keep breathing, keep still, [click], ease out, do not speed up”
“Keeping your head still, attempt to wrap your shoulder blades around your spine… there, lock it in place, [click], ease out”
Maintain consistent posture, head position, pace, and arm pad contact throughout
Only full range-of-motion reps with proper contraction count toward recorded total
Instructor may choose to continue set beyond concentric failure if under strict control and tension remains stimulative
For brand-new clients, full-range reps without failure may be sufficient based on form, tolerance, and experience level of client
Effort must increase throughout the set to maintain pace as fatigue rises; mechanical tension is created by matching effort to fatigue

sections.heading: Notes
items: Always point out overhead padded mechanism on entry and exit; cue “watch your head” for safety
Expect variability in client ROM; use first 2–3 reps to assess and establish individual expectations
Encourage full scapular retraction; avoid leaning back to move movement arms further
Simple Row is suitable for clients with hand, wrist, or elbow limitations and useful for improving posture
May pair with pulldown to complement upper back engagement, particularly due to lack of scapular retraction in pulldown
For clients with shoulder concerns, TSC may be appropriate:
Pin weight stack with movement arms at approximate midpoint to create an immovable load
Cue effort progression: 50% effort (30 sec), 75% effort (30 sec), all-out effort (30 sec) = 90 sec total; may use shorter durations to introduce
Helps strengthen shoulder and may eventually allow transition to dynamic execution
Estimated carryover of strength ~15° above and below static position
During early sessions with lighter weight, clients may perform more reps due to learn the movement/protocol with lower intensity
High rep volume may lead to discomfort before stimulation; Over time, look to progress to heavier weights (~10 reps max) as soon as control and tolerance to intensity is demonstrated
Aim for 6-second positive / 6-second negative cadence with appropriate intensity once form is consistent

cards.title: Torso Rotation – Quick Reference Guide
cards.intro: This is an abbreviated version of the understanding required of a MSF Exercise Practitioner. Please see Comprehensive Overview for more details.

sections.heading: Target Muscles
items: External Obliques – spinal rotation
Internal Obliques – spinal rotation

sections.heading: Synergists
items: Rotatores – spinal rotation
Hip Abductors – stabilize via hip horizontal abduction
Rectus Abdominis – spinal flexion / posterior pelvic tilt support

sections.heading: Considerations for Setup
items: Seat Position
Options
Positions 1 & 5 = largest rotation (most clients)
Positions 2 & 4 = reduced rotation (deconditioned or limited mobility)
Position 3 = neutral (not used for working sets)
Ensure seat is fully locked into stopper
Contraindication
Osteoporosis/Osteopenia
No dynamic rotation
Use Static Hold only if medically cleared
Leg Pads
Thin pads = standard
Thick pads = smaller clients or to increase stretch
Mixed pads possible but generally unnecessary
Arm Pads
Position 1 (default): lowest and closest (most clients)
Position 4: higher for taller clients while staying close to torso
Other positions only for wider clients needing more space
Entry & Safety
Warn client: “Watch your head” (overhead workbox)

sections.heading: Posture / Get Set
items: Pelvis fully back into seat and hip pads
Use seat belt if pelvis cannot stay stable
Knees abducted into pads, feet flat under knees
Use blocks if needed for shorter clients
Arms wrap over pads, forearms along pad, hands “cap” ends
Posterior pelvic tilt (“tightened down”)
Mid-back stays in contact with pad (rounded spine)

sections.heading: Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds
items: Load-Up (Critical Teaching Phase)
Cue: “Tighten/crunch down”
Maintain mid-back contact
Sequence
Draw far-side roller into body
Then rotate ribcage
Goal: attach carriage to ribcage before turning
Concentric (Rotation Phase)
Maintain posterior pelvic tilt (do not lift chest)
Emphasize
Compact movement = more tension
Not chasing ROM
Stop when
Obliques fully tightened (no further contraction possible)
Monitor
Hips stay back in pads
Knees don’t slide forward
Head
Follows torso or stays neutral
Never leads the movement
Arms
Do not create extra movement beyond ribcage
Upper Turnaround
Brief pause every rep
From rep 3+: 2–3 second squeeze
Purpose
Increase safety and control
Improve muscle awareness
Coaching must be specific
“Keep tight, keep breathing… ease out”
Not just “squeeze”
Eccentric (Return Phase)
Cue: “Ease out”
Lower body remains completely still
Rotate only through ribcage
Maintain tension while returning
Cue before bottom
“Only go far enough for weights to barely touch”
Lower Turnaround
At weight stack touch
Immediate but smooth direction change
No pause
Cue: “Drag through the bottom”
Key Technique Principles
Movement is driven by ribcage, not arms
Shorter ROM with higher tension is preferred
Stability of pelvis = better oblique loading
Avoid “reaching” or “turning as far as possible”
Programming Considerations
Train both directions
Reps: 4–7 per side (since exercise is doubled)
Avoid failure on first side
Rest enough to match reps on both sides
Final rep of first side: challenging but not failure
Special Population: Osteoporosis / Osteopenia
Default Approach
Avoid rotation entirely unless cleared
Static Hold (SH) Option (if cleared)
Seat at position 2 or 4
Carriage aligned square to torso
No movement at any time
Execution
Client braces and tightens midsection
Instructor performs interpersonal handoff
Hold: 20–60 seconds
Instructor controls load during unload
Key Rule
Zero movement during entire SH
Purpose: train safely without contraindicated rotation
Final Coaching Emphasis
Teach how to create tension, not just to move
Reinforce posture and control continuously
The goal is mechanical tension in the obliques, not maximal rotation or fatigue
